item.title: Nairobi is bulldozing the Kibera settlement for a housing project, but who really benefits?
item.description: Kenya’s plan for affordable homes aims to redevelop one of the country’s most visible symbols of urban poverty.
item.content:encoded:
Bulldozers and construction crews are reshaping parts of Nairobi’s best-known informal settlement, Kibera. In a video shared by President William Ruto, new apartment blocks rise alongside existing corrugated-iron structures, while new roads cut through the settlement. The message is clear: Kenya’s affordable housing programme is bringing modern housing to one of the country’s most visible symbols of urban poverty.

The redevelopment forms part of Ruto’s broader affordable housing programme, which aims to deliver 200,000 housing units annually, combining social housing, affordable homes and market-rate units. By March 2026, government figures indicated that 8,367 units had been completed since Ruto took office in September 2022, with many more at various stages of construction across the country. Completed units therefore remain well below the programme’s stated annual target.

Supporters see it as a long-overdue investment in urban infrastructure and housing. Critics, however, have challenged the compulsory levy used to finance the programme: employees pay 1.5% of their gross monthly salary, matched by a 1.5% employer contribution, while people outside formal employment pay 1.5% of their gross income. They have also raised concerns about whether the homes will be affordable to lower-income households and allocated transparently.

item.title: Horror fiction: On the Khangchendzonga slopes, barriers between the physical and spirit worlds melt
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Redtooth: A Himalayan Horror Story’, by Satyajit Sarna.

The wooden path in the forest was suddenly overhung with trees – sinister-looking, grasping, their gnarled hands reaching out. Rhododendrons! And so many of them! In bloom, this must be a mountainside of bright red – just blood-red flowers hanging overhead and on either side.

Which would “the multitudinous seas incarnadine”, he thought. Macbeth, from English class. He smiled, how deep the stamp of colonial schooling ran in his subconscious. “The multitudinous seas incarnadine, making the green one red.” The whole green, broad-leaved forest must be red in May, incarnadined.

“Look,” he pointed out to Mandhira, “the rhododendrons you wanted to see.”

“Oh, are these rhododendrons? I thought they’d be more like creepers.”

“Tree rhododendrons, different from other ones. I think those grow on creepers.”

“Didn’t Manish say they wouldn’t be around this season?”

item.title: Rural jobs fall nearly 50% in first month of VB-G RAM G: Report
item.description: The employment generation figures in July were the lowest in the last five years for both households and person-days.
item.content:encoded:
Employment generated under the government’s new rural job guarantee scheme fell by nearly half in July, the first month since it replaced the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme, The Indian Express reported on Monday.

Only 7.6 crore person-days were generated under the Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission Gramin Act, or VB-G RAM G, in July, as compared to 15.3 crore in the same month last year under MGNREGA, the newspaper cited official data.

A person-day refers to the amount of work done by one person in one working day. This means that a 20 person-day project can be completed by 20 people in one day, or one person in 20 days

The number of households that availed the rural employment guarantee scheme also fell by 51.4% to 68.9 lakh in July, compared with 1.4 crore under the old scheme in the same month last year.

The July figures for both households and person-days were the lowest in the last five years, reported The Indian Express.

The new scheme came into effect on July 1, replacing the two-decade-old MGNREGA.

item.title: Waste-to-energy plants are a disaster for the environment but India is building more
item.description: The incinerators have high capital costs and usually receive financial support from international institutions and subsidies in India.
item.content:encoded:
When Rajpal Saini retired from the Municipal Corporation of Delhi, he didn’t really plan to spend his golden years battling his former employer. But a waste incineration plant commissioned near his village, by the corporation, has made his life arduous.

“We have the entire waste processing mall of Delhi here – a khatta [dumping ground], a hazardous waste disposal site, a composting plant, and a 28 megawatt (MW) waste-to-energy plant. And as if all this were not enough, now they have imposed another one [WTE plant] on us,” said Saini, a resident of Sannoth, a village near Bawana at the northwestern edge of Delhi.

“The world recognises the value of yoga and breathing in fresh air. But forget about the outdoors; we even have to seal the holes in our doors to avoid the stench. My uncle, who regularly did pranayam [breathing exercises], has been paralysed and bedridden for six years now,” Saini said, whose car is full of posters advocating for the “right to breathe”.

item.title: ‘A lifetime of looking’: Arundhathi Subramanian on how Gieve Patel translated two Gujarati mystics
item.description: ‘Where the Creature Is, There Is the Creator: Poems by Akho and Vasto’ is Gieve Patel’s homage to the poets.
item.content:encoded:
It feels only right to begin with an admission: I don’t think I understood what Gieve Patel’s translations meant to him until he died.

And yet, he offered clues. He once said that his translations had come into his life as a replacement for his own poetry. On another occasion, he said that he would sometimes spend an entire day looking at a translation in much the way he contemplated a painting in his studio. At the end of it, he would often do no more than delete a comma. He frequently said that the work was almost done, that he was “months away from closure”. But then, he seemed to have been saying that for almost as long as I have known him.

I will admit I had my own theories about Gieve’s reluctance to publish his translations. I attributed it to a hyper-self-critical strain, a perfectionist’s pride. Or writer’s block. I thought he was overthinking things. At times, I wondered if he felt he had lost his earlier sure-footedness. Perhaps he was simply preoccupied with his painting? item.title: Lok Sabha passes bill to create panel for overseeing national tribunals
item.description: The members of the National Tribunals Commission, to be set up under the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026, will be appointed by the Union government.
item.content:encoded:
The Lok Sabha on Monday passed a bill to set up a central oversight body for appointing the chairpersons and members of the 16 tribunals in the country.

The body, named the National Tribunals Commission, will also review the performance of chairpersons and members of tribunals, as well as address complaints against them, according to the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026.

The Union government will appoint the chairperson and members of the commission in consultation with the chief justice of India.

Introducing the bill in the Lower House, Union Law and Justice Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal said that the legislation has been proposed to “ensure independence, transparency and uniformity in the qualifications, appointment, terms and conditions of service of chairpersons and members of various tribunals”.

If passed, it will repeal the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021.

This would be in line with the Supreme Court’s ruling on November 19, which said that certain provisions of the Act violated the principles of separation of powers and judicial independence. The court had also directed that a National Tribunals Commission be set up.

Among the tribunals covered under the legislation are the Central Administrative Tribunal, National Green Tribunal, Armed Forces Tribunal, Securities Appellate Tribunal, Debts Recovery Tribunals, National Company Law Appellate Tribunal and Income-tax Appellate Tribunal.

His remarks came even as the Israeli military has largely halted attacks in Gaza under pressure from Trump. Nikolay Mladenov, the Gaza envoy for Trump’s Board of Peace, said on Sunday that talks on the new roadmap to ending the conflict were still ongoing after meeting Netanyahu on Monday.

On July 30, Trump announced that the so-called Board of Peace had arrived at an agreement for the “complete disarmament” of Palestinian militant group Hamas and “all other armed” organisations operating in Gaza.

A day later, Hamas had said that it had agreed to the proposal, which would entail the group handing over its weapons and Israeli forces gradually withdrawing from the Gaza Strip.

The disarmament of Hamas had been among the sticking points in the peace deal moving forward.

item.description: An excerpt from ‘Steel Man: The Jatinder Mehra Legacy’, by Alison Norrington.

While his personal life was suffering immense tragedy, Jatinder Mehra’s tenure at Rourkela was also not without its challenges, particularly in dealing with the political influence of labour unions, a reality that had to be navigated with caution. The 1970s saw strong union activity, with frequent strikes and demands that often clashed with operational needs. These were defining moments that challenged Mehra’s ability to uphold operational integrity while prioritising worker safety. His time at Rourkela provided invaluable lessons in decision-making, negotiation, and the delicate balance of maintaining both discipline and fostering collaboration in a high-stakes industrial environment. “What I learned there shaped my future approach to management,” he reflects. “It wasn’t just about solving the immediate problems but about building systems that prevented them in the first place.” Mehra’s management philosophy became particularly important during his time at Rourkela, where the dynamics with the unions could sometimes be contentious. “In the 1970s, union power was strong, both in India and abroad. Abhirup Paul was arrested hours after he and another student of the institute were denied anticipatory bail by a Mumbai court. They were also booked for possessing downloaded books and other material that the prosecution alleged reflected Maoist ideology.

Paul was produced before a magistrate’s court on Saturday. The police sought 10 days’ custody, but the court remanded him to custody until Monday.

item.title: Assam: 100 dead in flood-related incidents
item.description: The flooding has affected 1.4 lakh persons in 10 districts.
item.content:encoded:
The toll from floods in Assam has risen to 100, with two deaths reported in the past 24 hours, the state disaster management authority said on Sunday.

Almost 1.4 lakh persons have been affected by the floods in 10 districts: Golaghat, Sivasagar, Hojai, Darrang, Lakhimpur, Jorhat, Karbi Anglong, Charaideo, Nagaon and Biswanath.

Golaghat is the worst hit, with around 70,000 people affected, followed by Sivasagar with nearly 40,000 and Jorhat with more than 16,000.

The Dhansiri river at Golaghat and Numaligarh, and the Kushiyara river at Sribhumi, are flowing above the danger mark.

“Due to a steady rise in the water level of Dhansiri in Golaghat district, people have been advised to stay away from the river,” PTI quoted an unidentified official of the disaster management authority as saying.

Nearly 49,100 people are staying in 125 relief camps and relief distribution centres in six districts, the news agency reported.

item.title: Should India apologise for caste injustice, like Nepal did?
item.description: A formal apology may not lead to concrete changes. Instead, pursuing reparations could help reimagine the project of social justice in India.
item.content:encoded:
“Why should I have to pay for something my ancestors did?” That is a refrain frequently heard from members of the upper castes during discussions about casteist violence and prejudice or reservations in India.

This belief has found renewed expression in the “Reservation Hatao Movement”, a social media campaign that gained visibility in late July. It calls for the abolition of caste-based reservation so that “merit” and equal competition can prevail.

Many Indians believe that caste is a relic of a bygone time and that the government’s social justice policies have addressed these problems.

This ignores the inherited control over land, wealth, education, social networks and institutions through which caste privilege reproduces itself, presenting outcomes produced by historical inequality as though they emerged from neutral competition among equals.

The Indian state, similarly, speaks the language of social justice without unsettling the structures of social power that shape Indian society.

It is against the backdrop of this refusal of historical accountability that Nepal’s decision to offer a formal state apology to Dalits for centuries of caste-based oppression acquired significance in India. In April, referring to Nepal’s decision, MP Chandrashekhar Azad asked in Parliament when India would apologise to Dalits for centuries of injustice.

item.title: How to make the most of boredom
item.description: Boredom may be good for us if we effectively tap into its full potential.
item.content:encoded:
Boredom is something many of us will do everything we can to avoid. We fill our time with social media, books and TV programmes and keeping our schedules packed with plans.

But boredom doesn’t always need to be seen as something negative. Boredom may, in fact, be good for you – but only if you effectively tap into its full potential.

1. It can push you towards positive change

Boredom tends to arise when we want to be mentally engaged but our current activity or environment isn’t providing the level of challenge, stimulation or meaning we need. This can leave us feeling restless – especially if we don’t know how to remedy the situation.

It’s for this reason that boredom can be used to push ourselves towards change and encourage exploration.

But in order to make boredom really work for you, it’s vital to avoid just reaching for the next easy distraction, like scrolling on your phone, online shopping or visiting the pantry for a snack.

Positive change comes not from asking “how do I stop feeling like this?” but asking yourself “what meaningful thing do I need next?” Focusing on doing something meaningful is key to making boredom a bridge to more productive or positive activities.

item.title: On India’s western coastline, ‘ghost’ fishing gear is causing marine pollution
item.description: Damaged nets and their pieces slip into the Arabian Sea where they continue trapping fish, turtles and other marine life.
item.content:encoded:
In the early light at Thoppumpady fishing harbour in the city of Kochi, coils of blue and green nylon nets lay heaped on the concrete docks, stiff with salt after a long night at sea. Many had been patched and repatched so often that they were barely holding together. Nets too damaged to mend are often cut loose offshore. Once they sink, few are ever recovered.

Across India’s west coast, lost fishing gear known as “ghost gear” has become a significant source of marine pollution. Nets vanish whole or in fragments, slipping into the waters of the Arabian Sea where they continue trapping fish, turtles and other marine life long after fishers abandon them.

India operates one of the world’s largest marine fishing sectors, supporting an estimated 14.5 million livelihoods along more than 7,500 kilometres of coastline.

While national estimates are scarce, a 2022 study in the southwestern state of Kerala, where Kochi is located, found that fishers lost, abandoned or discarded about 21% of their fishing gear annually. That’s more than 10 times the global average of 1.82% estimated by another study, which highlights the scale of material entering India’s marine environment.

The clarification came two days after the Lok Sabha passed the Taxation and Other Laws Amendment Bill 2026, which would allow banks and other service providers to levy charges on payments through UPI and RuPay debit cards.

The new bill would amend the Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007 and has led to fears that merchants, who would face a Merchant Discount Rate, would pass off the cost to consumers in the future.

The United Payment Interface, or UPI, is a real-time payment system. In July, users made 2,366 crore UPI transactions worth Rs 29.9 lakh crore.

Sharing its name with the coast of its origin, the language of Konkani is spoken in multiple dialects and written in scripts as diverse as Perso-Arabic, Roman, Devanagari, Kannada, and Malayalam. Enmeshed within the politics of language, so closely tied to regional identity in South Asia, official status, standardisation, and patronage pertaining to the scripts and languages in which Goan literary production occurs have been matters of long-standing concern in the enclave.

Located on the Konkan coast, Goa’s linguistic and literary heritage outsizes the region’s diminutive geography. Konkani is one of the languages in which Goan writers have expressed their craft in Romi and Nagri scripts, but Goan literature also appears in Marathi, English, and Portuguese. In fact, among the first novels of South Asian nascence is Os Brahmanes (1866) by Goan writer Francisco Luís Gomes (1829-1869); its Portuguese title really requires no translation, although The Brahmans (1971) – an edition in English – does exist.

Despite this varied literary heritage, in addition to the controversies surrounding it, intra- and inter-language translation in Goa has been limited. item.title: In photos: How festivals and rituals help Koraput’s Adivasis keep local seed varieties alive
item.description: On World Indigenous Peoples Day, a glimpse at how agricultural biodiversity is woven into everyday life, preserving local knowledge over generations.
item.content:encoded:
The first pot of rice newly harvested during October-November is never eaten straight away in Koraput. Before families gather around the meal, a portion is offered to the village deity. Around five to six months later, the next farming season begins with prayers for rain, while wooden ploughs, cattle and seeds are honoured in their own ceremonies.

In Koraput, in the Eastern Ghats of southern Odisha, every stage of cultivation has its own festival. The region is home to the Paroja, Gadaba, Kondh, Bhumia, Bhottada, Durua and Saura Adivasi communities. Here, agriculture is intrinsically linked with culinary heritage and faith.

Koraput is among India’s richest centres of crop diversity. It harbours hundreds of locally adapted crop varieties, including indigenous paddy, finger millet, little millet, pigeon pea, black gram, horse gram, niger, sesame, traditional vegetables, tubers and wild edible plants.

Unlike monoculture farming, fields here are planted with a diverse mix of crops that support one another, reduce farming risks and provide food throughout the year. Farmers cultivate varieties of rice that mature at different times, ensuring that all crops do not ripen at once. This helps spread the risk when rainfall is delayed or uneven.

item.title: ‘Iran’s Grand Strategy’: A nuanced understanding of how historical trauma is embedded in statecraft
item.description: Author Vali Nasr also draws attention to various hitherto lesser-known facts that show the state pragmatism behind Iranian defence policies.

Vali Nasr’s Iran’s Grand Strategy: A Political History is one of the most vital works that demand attention during the ongoing Iran-America standoff. The author argues that Iran’s strategy is not driven by ideology alone, but shaped by a collective memory of invasions, humiliation, foreign interference, and a deep-seated fear of national disintegration. To understand the politics of the Islamic regime, one has to understand the historical psychology behind it.

According to Nasr, the Islamic Republic views itself as both isolated and vulnerable because the Arab Sunni states surround it, while it possesses a distinct Persian identity fused with Shi’ism. Under the Safavids, especially Shah Ismail I, Shi’ism became Iran’s state religion as a strategic decision helping distinguish Iran from its Sunni Ottoman and Uzbek rivals. The Persian nationalism which in unique ways was subsumed in, as well as perpetuated by, Shia theocracy is distinctive to modern Iran. The United States is reviewing a proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period that allows certain foreign workers on non-immigrant visas to remain in the country and look for a new job after losing employment.

If finalised, foreign workers covered under the rule and their dependents would have to leave the US immediately if their employment ends before their authorised stay expires. They would be unable to change status or change employers within the country, unless US Citizenship and Immigration Services its discretion to forgive the lapse in status.

The 60-day grace period was introduced in 2017. It applies to several categories of temporary employment visas, including H-1B visas for workers in special occupations, L-1 visas for employees transferred within multinational companies, O-1 visas for persons with extraordinary ability.

The Department of Homeland Security has the discretion to shorten or refuse the grace period, although it has rarely done so, PTI reported.

The proposal from the Department of Homeland Security is currently under review by the federal Office of Management and Budget.

The details of the proposed regulation were not immediately known.

item.title: Does ‘training to failure’ build better muscle strength?
item.description: Stopping shortly before failure can preserve technique and reduce fatigue while providing an effective training stimulus.
item.content:encoded:
It is easy to assume that harder training always produces better results. In resistance training, which includes lifting weights or using resistance machines, taking every set to the point where you cannot complete another repetition may create more fatigue without producing better results.

A repetition, or rep, is one complete movement of an exercise. A set is a group of repetitions performed without a long rest.

Training to failure means continuing a set until you cannot complete another full repetition with acceptable technique, despite making your best effort. This is sometimes called momentary muscular failure.

An alternative is to stop while you could still perform one or more repetitions. This is described as repetitions in reserve, or RIR. If you could complete 10 repetitions but stop after eight, you have two repetitions in reserve, usually written as 2 RIR.

Why might training close to failure help?

Muscles are made up of individual cells called muscle fibres. These fibres are broadly classified as type 1 or type 2 fibres and are controlled by the nervous system. The type 2 fibres produce more force and can grow more than type 1 fibres.

item.title: Homer’s ‘Odyssey’: Who is Nausicaa, the bold princess who helped Odysseus go home?
item.description: It’s a shame Nausicaa was left out of Nolan’s ‘Odyssey’: she is a good example of how Homer’s Odyssey is ‘a woman’s poem’, as many scholars have recognised.

In Homer’s Odyssey, Nausicaa is a tall, gutsy teenage princess who finds a naked and helpless Odysseus washed up on her shore, gives him her brothers’ clothing, and instructs him on how to appeal to her mother, Queen Arete, for help to get home to Ithaca. She is crucial to his eventual return home after 20 years’ absence.

But she doesn’t appear in Christopher Nolan’s film at all – and her absence is part of a broader debate about how his version reduces or simplifies the role of women in the epic poem. In the Guardian, classicist Emily Hauser mourned the absence of the “delightfully brash princess”, along with nuance and complexity.

“There are more female characters than in most Nolan movies, thanks to the source material,” wrote classics professor Emily Wilson, whose translation of The Odyssey is a critically acclaimed bestseller, this week. “But none of them has much to say, in contrast to the characterisations in the poem.”

This applies to several key characters, from the enchantress Circe, who turned Odysseus’ men into pigs, to Odysseus’ wife Penelope. But what about the absent Nausicaa? Who was she? And why was she important?

On that August day in 1941, the monsoon skies had opened up, yet thousands of people turned up to pay their last respects to Bengal’s greatest creative artist and humanist. There was a time when writers would escape to the hills, spending their days with trees, streams, and wildlife, seeking inspiration for their art. This romantic notion of the hills is amply felt in literary works born from such circumstances, which in turn, compel the reader to believe that the mountains are sites of pristine beauty and undisturbed peace. Writings across genres – poetry, travelogue, fiction – unanimously agree that there are few things as majestic as a mountain. Gurgaon over many centuries was little more than a small rural hamlet in the periphery of the towering city of power Delhi. Across the ages possibly its best known resident was Hemu Vikramaditya, a general in the army of Sher Shah Suri who defeated the forces of Humayun and later Akbar. Gurgaon gained some modest standing only as the customary resting place for Akbar’s entourage when they marched to Amber.

Its fortunes altered after Independence. Badly singed by the fires of the Partition riots in 1947-’48, Gurgaon was substantially emptied of its Muslim population. But in the city of wealth and opportunities that Gurgaon metamorphosed into in recent decades, Muslims converged in droves. Yet they still struggle for dignity and rights in a habitat that they still find riven – under its skin-deep glitter – with prejudice and indifference.

This is mostly true, except perhaps in the case of legal history where the first draft is written in the records of the courts by its stenographers and judges. It is these records which capture the present and preserve it for posterity in public and private archives for historians of the future.

As the world moved into the digital age, the information technology revolution promised to make it easier than ever to store, index and organise records. item.title: Is it worse to eat junk food early in the day?
item.description: The body can process food more efficiently in the morning but blood sugar spikes and hunger pangs can quickly crop up after an unhealthy meal.
item.content:encoded:
Many of us have grown up with the mantra that breakfast is the most important meal of the day.

But whether it’s snatching an extra half hour of sleep, or focusing on getting the kids out of the house, there are various reasons why assembling a healthy breakfast might slip down your list of priorities – especially on a weekday.

So, is it worse to eat unhealthy foods first thing, compared to later in the day? And what about skipping breakfast altogether?

It’s not just about calories

You probably know eating foods high in sugar, salt and saturated fats – especially when they’re highly processed – puts you at greater risk of a range of serious health conditions. These include diabetes, heart disease and some cancers.

Poor diet can also affect our gut health, mental health and reproductive health.

item.title: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye sign defence pact amid conflict in West Asia
item.description: India said that it was ‘closely following’ the agreement.
item.content:encoded:
Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye on Friday signed a joint defence agreement on Friday, amid the conflict in West Asia.

India said that it was “closely following” the new defence pact.

The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, is aimed at “strengthening collective deterrence” and states that an armed attack against any one of the three countries would be considered an attack against all.

It also seeks to enhance defence cooperation among the three countries and promote peace, security and stability in the region and beyond.

However, the agreement does not specify detailed military commitments or obligations that have been accepted, Reuters reported.

An unidentified Turkish official told the news agency that the pact was “purely defensive in nature” and was not directed against any particular country.

The official added that the pact was open to other regional countries and would not replace existing bilateral or multilateral defence arrangements.

The agreement was signed by Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

It came against the backdrop of heightened tensions in West Asia amid conflict involving Iran, Israel and the United States.

The pact brings together three major Sunni Muslim-majority states: Saudi Arabia, the Gulf’s strongest economy, one of the world’s top oil exporters and home to Islam’s holiest sites, Pakistan, the only nuclear-armed Muslim-majority country and Türkiye, which has North Atlantic Treaty Organization’s second-largest military.

item.title: Nepal’s demolition drive leaves thousands homeless, violates human rights
item.description: The government and armed forces evicted mostly poor and marginalised residents of Kathmandu.
item.content:encoded:
The mass eviction of slums and informal settlements in Nepal’s capital Kathmandu and surrounding districts has displaced an estimated 15,000-20,000 people.

On April 25, the Nepal government began forcibly removing landless residents from the Kathmandu Valley, later extending the drive beyond the capital.

Nepal faces a staggering crisis: more than 3.5 million people are landless or homeless. A government commission invited applications for registration, and 1.2 million people – mostly poor, Dalit, and indigenous – have already registered in the hope of receiving land. Ironically, these communities have borne the brunt of evictions carried out without adequate notice, consultation, or alternative housing. The lack of support has eroded their trust in the state.

The ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party pledged to resolve landlessness within 1,000 days of office. Its 100-point action plan also promised relief to the landless. item.title: An evolutionary model that predates Darwin’s natural selection is making a comeback
item.description: Lamarckism contended that an organism may acquire characteristics in response to its environment and pass these on.
item.content:encoded:
Evolution is a fact of life. So much so that even the theory of evolution is evolving. Lately, a centuries-old discredited idea has been making a strong comeback. It helps us explain scientific observations that according to standard evolutionary theory should be impossible.

I’m referring to Lamarckism, named after theoretical proposals from French biologist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck in 1809. Lamarckism stands for the hypothesis that parents of a given organism may acquire or improve certain characteristics during their lifetimes in response to the demands of their environment. And they then somehow transmit those characteristics to their offspring, making those better able to cope with the same demands too.

Lamarck sought to explain why organisms and their environments fit so well together, and how organisms change over time, as observed in the fossil record. Of course, an alternative explanation was provided by Charles Darwin (and others) half a century later. Darwin’s ideas were built around natural selection, which says that some individuals within a species are born with differences that lead them to perform better and therefore reproduce more than others.

item.title: Cockroach movement claims victory but the odds are stacked against India’s youngsters
item.description: Four main issues of fairness in education and employment need to be addressed.

Over the past few weeks, young people have mobilised to protest India’s broken education system, against the background of a shortage of job opportunities.

The protests were initially sparked by the cancellation of a medical school entrance exam after questions were leaked, leading some despondent young people to take their own lives. The movement repurposed the image of a cockroach as their symbol – inspired by a comment by India’s chief justice, allegedly comparing jobless young people to “cockroaches”. Humour and satire were integral to the recent unrest.

On Saturday, the cockroach movement claimed its biggest victory since the protests began with the resignation of India’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan.

But this move will only do so much. These issues did not appear overnight, nor can they be easily fixed.

Irregularities and shortcomings in education, as well as rampant unemployment, have been major issues in northern India since at least the early 1970s.
